patches.new: Rotations and reflections are orthogonal matrices: each preserves lengths and angles, so it carries the standard unit vectors $(1,0,\dots)$, $(0,1,\dots)$, \dots, which are orthonormal, to an orthonormal set of images, and those images are exactly its columns.

patches.new: The singular values are unique: they are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$, and those eigenvalues are fixed by $A$ (they are the roots of the characteristic polynomial of $A^\top A$). When the \emph{nonzero} $\sigma_j$ are distinct, each $\sigma_j^2$ is a simple eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix $A^\top A$, so its unit eigenvector $v_j$ is unique up to sign, and $u_j = Av_j/\sigma_j$ is then fixed by $v_j$ (flipping the sign of both $u_j$ and $v_j$ leaves \cref{eq:least-squares-outer} unchanged). Singular vectors belonging to a repeated singular value, or to $\sigma_j = 0$ (the null directions), are not unique: any orthonormal basis of the corresponding space will do.

    s = np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False)
    ax.semilogy(np.arange(1, len(s) + 1), s/s[0], st, label='M = %d' % M)
ax.set_xlabel('index j'); ax.set_ylabel('sigma_j / sigma_1 (dimensionless)')
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which='both')
